articles.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
articles.excerpt: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

articles.title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
articles.excerpt: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $\Theta(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.

articles.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
articles.excerpt: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation \emph{prover awareness}: presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship. We formalize the privacy dimension as \emph{Enhanced Delegation Anonymity} (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, \emph{Proof-Carrying Credentials} (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation. Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.

articles.title: Rethinking the Temperature for Federated Heterogeneous Distillation
articles.excerpt: Federated Distillation (FedKD) relies on lightweight knowledge carriers like logits for efficient client-server communication. Although logit-based methods have demonstrated promise in addressing statistical and architectural heterogeneity in federated learning (FL), current approaches remain constrained by suboptimal temperature calibration during knowledge fusion. To address these limitations, we propose ReT-FHD, a framework featuring: 1) Multi-level Elastic Temperature, which dynamically adjusts distillation intensities across model layers, achieving optimized knowledge transfer between heterogeneous local models; 2) Category-Aware Global Temperature Scaling that implements class-specific temperature calibration based on confidence distributions in global logits, enabling personalized distillation policies; 3) Z-Score Guard, a blockchain-verified validation mechanism mitigating 44% of label-flipping and model poisoning attacks. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks with varying model/data heterogeneity demonstrate that the ReT-FHD achieves significant accuracy improvements over baseline methods while substantially reducing communication costs compared to existing approaches. Our work establishes that properly calibrated logits can serve as self-sufficient carriers for building scalable and secure heterogeneous FL systems.

articles.title: Add EIP: Bounded Storage Credit and Debit
articles.excerpt: We propose Bounded Storage Credit and Debit (#12707) as a successor to EIP-7519. SCREDIT adds an amount to a storage slot and SDEBIT subtracts an amount, each only if the slot’s value lies within a lower and an upper bound, given as operands, before and after the change. Both push a success flag, and neither pushes the slot’s value. A failed check leaves the slot unchanged and costs what a store of the unchanged value costs. The upper bound works with USDC’s balance layout, where the top bit of each balance word is a blacklist flag; the lower bound states floors such as a minimum balance. The success flag lets contracts keep their own error handling. We expect a small benefit for block validation once Glamsterdam’s block-level access lists are active. articles.title: ERC-8512: GPU Collateral Evidence
articles.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for a draft ERC, GPU Collateral Evidence. Summary GPUs have become loan collateral. Operators borrow against their fleets, financiers buy servers and lease them back, and on-chain lenders now fund GPU loans with stablecoins against tokenized titles. Every one of these deals rests on three facts the lender cannot see from where it sits: Is this GPU pledged to anyone else? Does it still exist? Did it actually serve compute this month? ERC-8512 gives each question a common, machine-readable answer: A device key for one physical GPU, derived from the identity key that data-centre GPUs carry from the factory and use to answer attestation challenges. articles.excerpt: Discussion thread for EIP-8513, Add EIP: Pre-seeded Encrypted Execution Payloads by cskiraly · Pull Request #12706 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub . Under EIP-7732 a builder is expected to wait for attestations to show that the block will stay before it reveals the execution payload. The payload’s transfer therefore starts at the reveal and has to reach the PTC before the payload deadline, and the time from the block to the reveal carries nothing of it, although the bid has already fixed its contents. This EIP lets the builder send the payload encrypted as soon as a valid block includes its bid. The reveal becomes a 32-byte key.
